Causes : Pre-renal failure : Hypovolemia, low cardiac output, renovascular obstruction.
Intra-renal failure : Acute tubular necrosis (ischemic/toxic), glomerulonephritis, interstitial nephritis.
Post-renal failure : Urinary obstruction (e.g., prostate enlargement, stones).
Distinguishing Pre-renal vs. Intra-renal Failure : Test Pre-Renal Intra-Renal Urine Na⁺ (mMol/L) < 20 40 Urine/Plasma Osmolality Ratio 1.4 < 1.1 Urine/Plasma Urea Ratio 14 < 10
Definition : Urine <450 mL/day + rising urea (normally 1.7-6.7 mMol/L)
Urea rise : 5 mMol/L/day (up to 15 in surgery/trauma/bleeding)

Fluid Overload: Exercise extreme caution with aggressive fluids in patients with severe malaria (risk of non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema) and acute renal failure.
Hypercalcaemia: Intravenous bisphosphonates (e.g., zoledronic acid); calcitonin — Hydration status, urine output, renal function — Bisphosphonates contraindicated in severe acute renal failure
Tumour lysis syndrome – acute renal failure, electrolyte disturbances; mitigated by prophylaxis.
Acute hemolytic reaction: Can lead to acute renal failure, DIC, death if untreated — Strict ABO/Rh matching, double‑check patient ID
Scleroderma renal crisis: Acute renal failure, malignant hypertension — Daily BP, renal panel

ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: Acute renal failure (now called acute kidney injury) is a rapid loss of kidney function, marked by low urine output and rising blood urea. It can be pre‑renal, intra‑renal or post‑renal and requires prompt identification of cause and supportive care.

sections.p: AKI is defined by any of: urine output <450 mL/24 h, increase in serum creatinine ≥0.3 mg/dL within 48 h, or rise in creatinine to ≥1.5 × baseline within 7 days.
b: Use KDIGO criteria for staging
Measure urine output hourly in at‑risk patients

t.b: Is kidney filtration falling? A rise confirms AKI; baseline needed for staging
Is the patient oliguric? <0.5 mL/kg/h for 6 h signals AKI

sections.p: KDIGO stages 1‑3 use creatinine rise and urine output thresholds; stage 3 includes need for renal replacement therapy.
b: Stage 1: Cr ↑ 0.3 mg/dL or 1.5‑1.9 × baseline
Stage 2: Cr 2.0‑2.9 × baseline
Stage 3: Cr ≥3.0 × baseline or <0.3 mL/kg/h ≥24 h

sections.p: Classify by location of the problem: pre‑renal (decreased perfusion), intra‑renal (parenchymal damage), post‑renal (obstruction). In low‑resource settings add tropical infections.
b: Pre‑renal: hypovolemia (diarrhoea, malaria), low cardiac output, sepsis
Intra‑renal: acute tubular necrosis (ischemia, nephrotoxins, malaria), glomerulonephritis, interstitial nephritis, sickle‑cell crisis
Post‑renal: urinary obstruction from stones, enlarged prostate, schistosomal fibrosis

sections.p: Patients may be oliguric or non‑oliguric, with swelling, nausea, confusion, and lab evidence of rising urea/creatinine. Malaria‑related AKI often shows dark urine from haemoglobinuria.
b: Reduced urine volume
Peripheral edema
Hypertension or hypotension depending on cause

sections.p: Targeted tests clarify cause, severity and guide therapy.
b: Prioritise bedside urine analysis when labs unavailable

t.a: Urine sodium and fractional excretion of sodium (FeNa)
t.b: Pre‑renal vs intra‑renal? FeNa <1 % suggests pre‑renal; >2 % suggests tubular injury
Casts present? Muddy brown granular casts point to ATN; RBC casts suggest glomerulonephritis
Is there obstruction? Detects hydronephrosis; if unavailable, assess bladder scan

t.a: Serology for malaria, HIV, hepatitis B
t.b: Is an infectious trigger present? Positive test directs specific therapy

sections.p: Uncorrected AKI can rapidly lead to life‑threatening complications.
b: Severe hyperkalemia → cardiac arrest
Pulmonary edema → respiratory failure
Metabolic acidosis → shock

sections.p: Treat the underlying cause first, then support kidney function and prevent further injury.
b: Fluid resuscitation for hypovolemia; use isotonic crystalloids, avoid overload
Avoid nephrotoxins (aminoglycosides, NSAIDs, herbal nephrotoxins)
Diuretics only if volume‑overloaded and urine output remains low
Renal replacement therapy when refractory hyperkalemia, acidosis, or fluid overload

sections.p: Monitor renal function daily until stable, educate on hydration, avoid nephrotoxins, and vaccinate against hepatitis B.
b: Re‑measure creatinine at 48 h and 7 days
Educate patients on early signs of dehydration

sections.p: Conditions that mimic AKI but have different management.
b: Chronic kidney disease flare (baseline creatinine already high)
Urinary tract infection causing transient oliguria

sections.p: Certain values may appear normal despite injury.
b: FeNa can be falsely low in early ATN if diuretics used
Serum urea may stay normal in low‑protein diets

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden loss of urine, severe swelling, confusion, or chest pain indicating hyperkalemia

faq.q: Why is urine output important in AKI?
faq.a: It reflects real‑time kidney perfusion and filtration; falling output often precedes lab changes.
Yes, many patients improve with cause‑directed therapy and fluid management if complications are avoided.

faq.q: What makes malaria a common cause of AKI in the tropics?
faq.a: Severe hemolysis, dehydration, and microvascular obstruction damage renal tubules.

exam: Explain how to differentiate pre‑renal AKI from acute tubular necrosis using urine studies.
